stem: A developer adds detailed comments in a tool's Python source file explaining exactly when to call `create_ticket` versus `update_ticket`, but leaves the `description` field passed to the model as a one-word summary for each ("Creates a ticket." / "Updates a ticket."). Misrouting continues. What's the most likely reason?

options.text: The model only sees the tool's `description`, `name`, and `input_schema` — never the source file or its comments
options.explanation: Correct — the model's only view of a tool is its declared interface, not the code or comments behind it.

options.text: The two tools must have overlapping `input_schema` types, which is what's really driving the mismatch
options.explanation: Nothing here suggests a schema conflict — the stated fix attempt was comments, and the real gap is what the model can actually see.

options.text: Comments only help once the tools have been used successfully at least once, since the model learns from execution history
options.explanation: The model doesn't learn tool behavior from past runs mid-session — comments never reach it at all, regardless of usage history.

options.text: The order of `create_ticket` and `update_ticket` in the tools array determines which one wins on ambiguous phrasing
options.explanation: Array order isn't a selection signal the model reasons over.

keyPrinciple: The model only ever sees a tool's name, description, and input schema — not its implementation or comments.

stem: Two tools, `archive_ticket` and `close_ticket`, both accept a numeric `ticket_id`, and both descriptions currently read "Marks a ticket as done." What single addition would most reduce misrouting between them?

options.text: A longer list of synonyms for "done" added to each description
options.explanation: More synonyms for the same vague word doesn't tell the model which tool to prefer for a given case.

options.text: A sentence stating the distinct outcome of each and when to prefer one over the other
options.explanation: Correct — a boundary statement naming the real difference is exactly what separates two overlapping tools.

options.text: Renaming both tools to start with the same verb so the model recognizes them as a pair
options.explanation: Matching prefixes would make the two names harder to tell apart, not easier.

options.text: Increasing the model's max output tokens so it has more room to reason before calling a tool
options.explanation: Output length isn't related to how the model distinguishes two tool descriptions.

keyPrinciple: A boundary sentence stating the distinct outcome of each tool is what separates near-identical descriptions.

stem: A developer renames the internal function implementing a tool from `fetch_data_v2` to `get_customer_record`, hoping this will help Claude choose it correctly, but leaves the tool's `description` field unchanged. What effect will this have on tool selection?

options.text: It will help immediately, since the model can now infer intent from the more descriptive function name
options.explanation: The model has no visibility into the internal function name at all, so there's nothing to infer from.

options.text: It will hurt selection, because two names now effectively refer to the same tool
options.explanation: The model isn't aware of the internal name, so it can't create a conflict the model would notice.

options.text: None — the model only sees the `name`, `description`, and `input_schema` it was given
options.explanation: Correct — internal implementation naming is invisible to the model; only the declared interface matters.

options.text: It will help only after the next deployment, once the API re-indexes function signatures
options.explanation: There's no such re-indexing step, and the internal name was never part of what the model sees to begin with.

keyPrinciple: Renaming internal implementation details does nothing for tool selection; only the declared interface matters.

stem: `send_message` is described as "Sends a message and returns delivery status." `post_update` is described as "Sends an update and returns delivery status." Both take the same `channel` and `text` parameters, and requests keep routing to whichever tool happens to run first, regardless of content. What's the most direct fix?

options.text: Increase the model's `temperature` so it considers more options before committing to a tool call
options.explanation: Temperature affects wording variety, not whether the model has enough information to distinguish two tools.

options.text: Merge both into a single tool with a `mode` parameter, without changing the vague description text
options.explanation: This moves the ambiguity inside one tool's parameter instead of resolving it, and the model still has to guess the mode correctly.

options.text: Add a retry policy so the system automatically calls the other tool afterward if the first one seems wrong
options.explanation: This reacts after a wrong call instead of preventing the misrouting, and adds infrastructure for a problem two sentences of text can fix.

options.text: State concretely what each tool consumes and where it applies, so the wording itself removes the overlap
options.explanation: Correct — naming the concrete input type and boundary is what turns two near-identical descriptions into distinguishable ones.

keyPrinciple: Near-identical descriptions need a concrete input type and boundary statement, not more infrastructure around the call.

stem: `manage_ticket` currently handles creating tickets, editing fields, closing tickets, and reassigning owners, all through one input schema with many optional fields. Requests like "reassign ticket 500 to Priya" sometimes create a duplicate ticket instead. What's the most effective redesign?

options.text: Split `manage_ticket` into `create_ticket`, `edit_ticket`, `close_ticket`, and `reassign_ticket`
options.explanation: Correct — this is the documented fix for one tool covering too many unrelated jobs: give each job its own narrow tool.

options.text: Keep one tool, but add a required `action` enum field the model must fill correctly on every call
options.explanation: This still leaves one generic tool whose intent the model must reason about correctly filling in, rather than tools whose name already states the job.

options.text: Rename `manage_ticket` to `ticket_operations` so its scope reads as clearer
options.explanation: A broader-sounding name doesn't narrow what the tool actually does or fix the schema ambiguity.

options.text: Add more example phrasings to the system prompt showing the correct `action` value for each request type
options.explanation: This targets wording for specific phrasings rather than fixing the tool's contract, so it won't generalize to new phrasings.

keyPrinciple: Split a tool that covers too many unrelated jobs into purpose-specific tools with narrow contracts.

stem: A system prompt instructs: "Whenever the user asks about billing, use the account tool." The team has `get_account_summary` (an identity/profile lookup) and `update_billing_address` (a workflow tool with side effects). After this instruction ships, the model starts calling `update_billing_address` for plain billing questions where no address change was requested. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: The two tools must share the same `input_schema`, which is what's really driving the mismatch
options.explanation: Nothing in the scenario suggests a schema conflict — the trigger described is the wording of the system prompt itself.

options.text: The prompt's keyword ("billing") matches more strongly than the tool descriptions' boundaries
options.explanation: Correct — keyword-sensitive system prompt wording can quietly override even well-written tool descriptions.

options.text: `tool_choice` is set to `{"type": "any"}`, forcing some tool call regardless of the system prompt
options.explanation: Forcing any tool call doesn't explain why this specific tool wins over the more appropriate one — the wording is the deciding factor.

options.text: The system prompt has no real effect on tool selection; only descriptions and schemas matter
options.explanation: System prompt wording absolutely can steer tool selection — this scenario is a direct example of that.

keyPrinciple: Keyword-sensitive system prompt wording can override even a carefully written tool description.

stem: A `notify_user` tool has grown to handle sending emails, SMS, and push notifications, all through a `channel` string parameter with subtly different required fields per channel. The model frequently omits a required field for the SMS case specifically. What's the most effective redesign, following the same principle used to fix an overloaded document-analysis tool?

options.text: Add a `required_fields` list to the description enumerating every field required for every channel
options.explanation: This documents the complexity without removing it — the model still has to apply the right subset correctly on every call.

options.text: Rename `notify_user` to `notify_user_v2` to signal that it was updated
options.explanation: A version suffix says nothing about which fields apply to which channel.

options.text: Split `notify_user` into `send_email`, `send_sms`, and `send_push`, each with its own required fields
options.explanation: Correct — splitting a tool whose requirements vary sharply by mode into mode-specific tools removes the conditional-field guesswork entirely.

options.text: Remove the SMS channel entirely until a dedicated tool can be built
options.explanation: This drops needed capability instead of fixing the tool's contract for the case that's failing.

keyPrinciple: When one tool's requirements vary sharply by an internal mode, split it into mode-specific tools instead of one tool with conditional fields.

stem: A `process_payment` tool call returns `{"isError": false, "content": {"status": "declined", "reason": "insufficient_funds"}}`. Should the agent treat this as a failed tool call?

options.text: Yes — any response content that merely contains the word "declined" anywhere should be treated as `isError: true`
options.explanation: The `isError` flag, not keyword-matching the content, is what tells the agent whether the call itself failed.

options.text: It depends on whether `content` happens to be valid JSON
options.explanation: JSON validity has nothing to do with whether a call is treated as failed.

options.text: Only if the agent has already retried the call once before
options.explanation: Retry history doesn't change what a single response's `isError` flag means.

options.text: No — `isError` is false, so the call succeeded; the decline is business information, not a tool failure
options.explanation: Correct — the call reached the system and executed correctly; the decline is a business outcome, not a call failure.

keyPrinciple: isError signals whether the call itself succeeded, not whether the business outcome was favorable.

stem: An automation calls `create_ticket` using a service account that lacks a required scope, and the API returns an access-denied error. A developer wires up an exponential-backoff retry loop for it. What's wrong with that fix?

options.text: Permission errors aren't retryable; the same credentials will fail again no matter how long it waits
options.explanation: Correct — access-denied failures need a scope or credential change, which retrying can never produce on its own.

options.text: Exponential backoff only ever applies to validation-category errors, never to any other error category
options.explanation: Backoff is the pattern for transient errors, not validation errors — this mischaracterizes both categories.

options.text: The retry loop will eventually succeed once enough attempts have been made
options.explanation: Nothing about the account's permissions changes between attempts, so retrying more times won't produce a different outcome.

options.text: Access-denied errors always resolve themselves once a token cache refreshes
options.explanation: A missing scope isn't a caching issue — refreshing a token doesn't grant access it was never given.

keyPrinciple: Permission errors need escalation, not backoff — retrying with the same credentials changes nothing.

stem: A refund request exceeds a $500 policy threshold and is correctly rejected by business logic. Which error category best fits?

options.text: Business
options.explanation: Correct — the request was well-formed; it was rejected by a policy rule, which is the business category.

options.text: Transient
options.explanation: There's no timeout or service unavailability here — the call reached the system and was correctly rejected.

options.text: Validation
options.explanation: The input wasn't malformed; it was a valid request that a business rule rejected.

options.text: Permission
options.explanation: Access wasn't denied — the rejection is a policy decision on a well-formed, authorized request.

keyPrinciple: A policy rejection on a well-formed request is a business error, not validation or permission.

stem: A teammate proposes this response shape for every MCP tool failure: `{"isError": true, "content": "Something went wrong. Please try again."}`. Compared to categorized metadata (`errorCategory`, `isRetryable`), what will the agent be unable to do with this shape?

options.text: Know that the call failed at all, since `isError` is absent from this shape
options.explanation: `isError` is actually present and set to true here — the problem is what's missing beyond it, not the flag itself.

options.text: Decide whether to retry, adjust the request, or escalate beyond "it failed"
options.explanation: Correct — without a category or retryability flag, the agent has nothing to reason from except a generic failure notice.

options.text: Parse the response as valid JSON, since a plain string inside `content` isn't valid JSON syntax
options.explanation: A string value is valid JSON content — the issue is informational, not syntactic.

options.text: Relay any message to the user, since MCP blocks generic failure text from being shown
options.explanation: MCP doesn't block relaying a message — the problem is that this message gives the agent nothing to act on.

keyPrinciple: Uniform error responses prevent the agent from making an appropriate recovery decision.

stem: A `charge_card` tool's failure response includes `errorCategory: "business"` and `isRetryable: false`, but the `message` field just says "Failed." What does this response still fail to give the agent?

options.text: An `isError` flag, since categorized responses don't need one
options.explanation: Categorized responses still need `isError`; that's not what's missing here.

options.text: A `partial_results` field, since every categorized response must include one
options.explanation: Not every error response requires partial results — this isn't a subagent propagation case.

options.text: A human-readable explanation of why the business rule rejected the call
options.explanation: Correct — categorization tells the agent not to retry, but a customer-facing reason still needs an actual explanation in the message.

options.text: A numeric HTTP status code, since `errorCategory` alone isn't standards-compliant
options.explanation: An HTTP status code isn't part of the documented pattern here, and it wouldn't supply the missing explanation anyway.

keyPrinciple: Pair a business-error category with a real, customer-facing explanation, not just a category label.

stem: A `search_orders` tool is implemented so that both "zero orders match this filter" and "the orders database timed out" return the exact same response: `{"isError": false, "content": {"orders": []}}`. What downstream problem does this design create?

options.text: It's fine, since an empty array is always unambiguous regardless of why it's empty
options.explanation: This is exactly the problem — the same empty array can mean two very different things here.

options.text: It only matters if the agent needs to log the response for auditing
options.explanation: The issue affects the agent's real-time decision-making, not just later log review.

options.text: It's a performance problem, not a correctness problem, since both paths return quickly
options.explanation: Response speed isn't the concern — the concern is that the two outcomes are indistinguishable.

options.text: The agent will treat a real access failure as a confident "there is nothing here"
options.explanation: Correct — collapsing an access failure into the same shape as a genuine empty result hides a failure as a stronger, wrong claim.

keyPrinciple: Distinguish access failures (need a retry decision) from valid empty results (a successful query with no matches).

stem: A `send_email` tool call completes and the email is queued successfully, but the response comes back as `{"isError": true, "content": "Email queued for delivery"}`. Given only this response, what should a well-behaved agent do?

options.text: Treat the call as failed — `isError: true` is the flag the agent trusts, not the message text
options.explanation: Correct — the standardized flag is the signal to act on, even when the accompanying text reads like a success.

options.text: Treat it as successful, since the message text itself clearly describes a successful outcome
options.explanation: Trusting the message text over the flag is backwards — the flag is the documented, reliable signal.

options.text: Wait for a follow-up tool call before deciding anything
options.explanation: There's no such waiting step described — the agent should act on the response it already has.

options.text: Ignore the flag and re-parse the `content` string every time to decide
options.explanation: This defeats the purpose of having a standardized flag at all, and is more fragile than trusting it.

keyPrinciple: isError is the flag the agent trusts, even when the accompanying message text seems to describe success.

stem: A deployment agent is given all 14 tools available across three connected systems (build, deploy, monitoring), even though its actual job only ever needs 3 of them. Selection among just those 3 relevant tools becomes less reliable after the change. Why?

options.text: The three relevant tools must have overlapping `input_schema` fields
options.explanation: Nothing in the scenario points to a schema conflict among the three tools themselves.

options.text: Every tool adds decision-complexity overhead, degrading selection even among the tools it needs
options.explanation: Correct — tool count is a reliability variable; irrelevant tools degrade selection among the relevant ones too.

options.text: The monitoring tools are outdated and confusing the agent's date parsing
options.explanation: This invents a specific implementation defect the scenario gives no evidence for.

options.text: It's just a coincidence — tool count only ever affects latency, and never affects selection accuracy at all
options.explanation: The scenario is a direct example of tool count affecting selection reliability, not just speed.

keyPrinciple: Too many tools on one agent degrades selection reliability by increasing decision complexity, even for tools it needs.

stem: A report-generation agent is given a raw `run_sql_query` tool "in case it's ever useful." Logs later show it sometimes writes and runs its own SQL query instead of asking the data-analysis agent for an aggregated result, duplicating work. What principle explains this?

options.text: The reporting agent was specifically trained to prefer SQL over delegation
options.explanation: No such training preference is described — the risk comes from the tool's mere availability.

options.text: `tool_choice` defaults to forcing every available tool to be called once per session automatically
options.explanation: No `tool_choice` setting works this way.

options.text: A tool present in an agent's list is implicitly an invitation to use it, even outside its role
options.explanation: Correct — agents with tools outside their specialization tend to reach for them, causing exactly this kind of role drift.

options.text: MCP requires every connected tool to be exercised before a session ends
options.explanation: There's no such requirement in MCP.

keyPrinciple: Agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them.

stem: A triage agent is scoped only to a `classify_ticket` tool. A teammate suggests also giving it `close_ticket`, "in case a ticket turns out to be spam and can just be closed immediately." What risk does this specific addition introduce?

options.text: None — extra tools on the list never affect an agent's behavior unless it's explicitly told to use them
options.explanation: A tool's mere presence in an agent's list already creates the opportunity to use it, regardless of instructions.

options.text: It would only matter if `close_ticket` and `classify_ticket` shared the same input schema
options.explanation: The risk here is about role scope, not schema overlap between the two tools.

options.text: It's required, since every agent must have at least one write-capable tool
options.explanation: There's no such requirement — a triage agent's role can be fully served by a read/classify-only tool set.

options.text: It gives the triage agent an action tool outside its role, able to close tickets it should only classify
options.explanation: Correct — this is the risk of cross-specialization tool access: the agent can now act, not just classify.

keyPrinciple: Scope each agent's tools to exactly what its role needs; an agent can't misuse a tool it was never given.

stem: A summarization agent frequently needs to convert currency figures — roughly 70% of its outputs. Routing every conversion through the coordinator to a finance-data agent adds 2-3 round trips each time. The team gives the summarization agent one narrow `convert_currency` tool instead, and still routes anything more complex (historical rate lookups, multi-step conversions) through the coordinator as before. What principle does this follow?

options.text: Least privilege for a high-frequency common case, not general finance-data access
options.explanation: Correct — this scopes the exception to exactly the common case, while the rarer complex cases still go through the full mediated path.

options.text: Batching — the agent should instead collect all conversions and send them to the coordinator in one request at the end
options.explanation: Batching would delay results within the same pass and doesn't address the round-trip overhead described.

options.text: Full access is safer here, since the summarization agent already needs some financial data anyway
options.explanation: This over-provisions capability sized for the rare complex case onto an agent that only needs the simple, frequent one.

options.text: Speculative caching of likely currency values ahead of time, so no tool call is needed at all
options.explanation: Pre-guessing values can't reliably predict actual conversion needs, and unused cached values are wasted effort.

keyPrinciple: Give an agent scoped cross-role tools only for its high-frequency common case; route the rest through the coordinator.
sourceRef: Exam Guide TS 2.3; Exam Guide Sample Q9

stem: A form-filling agent must always produce a structured field extraction on a given turn — a plain-text reply isn't acceptable — but any of its three extraction tools would satisfy the requirement equally well. Which `tool_choice` setting guarantees this without dictating which specific tool runs?

options.text: `{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_fields_v1"}`
options.explanation: This forces one specific tool, which is more than needed when any of the three would work.

options.text: `{"type": "any"}`
options.explanation: Correct — "any" guarantees some tool call happens, letting the model still pick which of the three fits best.

options.text: `{"type": "auto"}`
options.explanation: "auto" still permits a plain-text reply, which is exactly what needs to be ruled out here.

options.text: Leaving `tool_choice` unset with all three tools defined
options.explanation: Leaving it unset behaves like "auto" by default and doesn't guarantee a tool call.

keyPrinciple: tool_choice: "any" guarantees a tool call, letting the model pick which one when several would satisfy it.

stem: A project merges three specialized agents into one "generalist" agent with all 20 of their combined tools. Response quality on previously-reliable single-role tasks drops, even though no individual tool changed. What best explains this?

options.text: The merge must have introduced a bug in the individual tool implementations
options.explanation: No tool itself changed, so an implementation bug doesn't fit what's described.

options.text: It's completely unrelated to raw tool count; the generalist agent simply needs a much larger context window
options.explanation: The scenario describes a selection-reliability drop, which context window size doesn't explain.

options.text: Tool count itself is a reliability variable — more tools degrade selection even for tools already used reliably
options.explanation: Correct — this is the same principle as giving one agent too many tools: the extra options are decision overhead on every turn.

options.text: Reliability only drops if the merged tools have colliding names
options.explanation: The scenario doesn't mention name collisions, and the degradation described applies even to tools that were already working.

keyPrinciple: Tool count is a reliability variable — more tools on an agent degrades selection among all of them, not just capability.

stem: A team adds a new MCP server for their internal wiki to the project config. Without any additional registration step, the next Claude Code session run against that project immediately lists new wiki-related tools. What explains this?

options.text: The tools were already built into Claude Code and just needed the wiki server's name to unlock them
options.explanation: These are new, server-specific tools, not pre-existing built-in ones waiting to be unlocked.

options.text: Claude Code caches all possible MCP tools in advance and reveals them once a matching server name appears
options.explanation: There's no such advance-caching mechanism — tools come from the server itself.

options.text: The tools only appear after the agent's first failed call to a similar built-in tool
options.explanation: Discovery isn't tied to a prior failed call — it happens at connection time.

options.text: Discovery happens automatically when the agent connects to the server, with no manual registration
options.explanation: Correct — this is exactly why the new tools appear immediately, with no separate registration.

keyPrinciple: MCP tools are discovered automatically at connection time.

stem: A five-person team all needs the same internal deployment-tracker MCP server as soon as they clone the repo, with no individual setup step. Where should this server be configured?

options.text: Project-scoped `.mcp.json`, so it's version-controlled and shared with everyone who clones the repo
options.explanation: Correct — this is exactly the shared, team-wide tooling case `.mcp.json` is for.

options.text: Each individual developer's own `~/.claude.json`, then copied by hand to every other teammate's machine
options.explanation: This defeats the purpose of shared config — every future change would need manual re-copying.

options.text: A `.env` file checked into the repository alongside the rest of the project's source code
options.explanation: `.env` isn't an MCP server configuration mechanism.

options.text: The root `CLAUDE.md` file, under a new `mcpServers` heading
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md holds project instructions, not MCP server definitions.

keyPrinciple: Project-scoped .mcp.json is for shared team tooling, version-controlled with the repo.

stem: A developer disconnects and reconnects to an MCP server mid-session, after the server has added two new tools. Does the agent need any manual step to see the new tools on reconnect?

options.text: Yes — each new tool must be manually registered in the project config before it's visible
options.explanation: There's no manual per-tool registration step in MCP.

options.text: No — discovery happens automatically at connection time, on every reconnect
options.explanation: Correct — discovery is tied to the connection event itself, not to any manual step.

options.text: Yes — the agent must be restarted from a fresh install for new tools to appear
options.explanation: A full reinstall isn't required; reconnecting to the server is enough.

options.text: No, but only if the tools were added before the very first connection of the day
options.explanation: There's no time-of-day condition on discovery — it happens at connection, whenever that occurs.

keyPrinciple: MCP tools are discovered automatically at connection time.

stem: A reviewer sees a committed `.mcp.json` with `"env": { "SLACK_TOKEN": "${SLACK_TOKEN}" }` and flags it as a leaked secret, asking for it to be scrubbed from git history. Is the reviewer right?

options.text: Yes — anything at all placed inside an `env` block in a committed file counts as a hardcoded secret
options.explanation: An `env` block referencing a placeholder isn't the same as a hardcoded value — the syntax matters.

options.text: It depends on whether `SLACK_TOKEN` is also defined in a `.env` file elsewhere in the repo
options.explanation: Whether another file also references the variable name doesn't change what this specific syntax does.

options.text: No — `${SLACK_TOKEN}` is a placeholder expanded from an environment variable, never a literal token
options.explanation: Correct — this is exactly what environment variable expansion is for: keeping the real secret out of version control.

options.text: Yes, but only because the variable name matches the service name
options.explanation: The variable's name doesn't determine whether a real secret is present — the placeholder syntax does.

keyPrinciple: Environment variable expansion (${VAR}) keeps secrets out of version-controlled MCP config.

stem: A solo contractor spins up a personal MCP server that queries their own invoicing tool, used only by them, and mistakenly commits it into the project's `.mcp.json` instead of `~/.claude.json`. The next teammate who pulls the repo now sees an invoicing tool with no credentials for it, and every session logs a connection error. What's the fix?

options.text: Add the contractor's personal credentials to the project's `.env` file so everyone can use it
options.explanation: This spreads a personal credential to the whole team for a tool that isn't meant to be shared at all.

options.text: Leave it in `.mcp.json` as-is, since removing a working server would break the contractor's own workflow
options.explanation: Leaving it there keeps producing connection errors for every other teammate — the server just doesn't belong in the shared config.

options.text: Rename the server entry so teammates don't notice the connection error
options.explanation: This hides the symptom without fixing the actual scope mismatch.

options.text: Move it to user-scoped `~/.claude.json`, since it's personal and doesn't belong in the shared config
options.explanation: Correct — a personal, single-user server belongs in user scope; putting it there stops the errors for everyone else.

keyPrinciple: A personal or experimental server that ends up in the shared project config breaks the build for everyone else — move it to user scope.

stem: An agent connected to a project-management MCP server calls a `list_all_items` tool three separate times per session just to learn what boards and columns exist, before it can make a targeted query. What would reduce this repeated discovery cost?

options.text: Expose the structure as an MCP resource the agent can read directly, instead of rediscovering it
options.explanation: Correct — resources let the agent read a content catalog once, instead of paying for exploratory tool calls every session.

options.text: Renaming `list_all_items` to something shorter so it's faster to call
options.explanation: A shorter name doesn't reduce how many times the tool needs to be called.

options.text: Adding `tool_choice: {"type": "any"}` so the agent is forced to call the right one the first time
options.explanation: Forcing a tool call doesn't reduce how many separate calls are needed to rediscover the same structure.

options.text: Removing `list_all_items` entirely, since resources always replace tools outright
options.explanation: Resources complement tools; removing the tool outright isn't necessary or implied.

keyPrinciple: MCP resources expose content catalogs to reduce exploratory tool calls.

stem: A config key needs to be renamed across a codebase, but you first need to find which files even reference it. Which pair of tools fits, in order?

options.text: Glob to find the files, then Bash to rename the key everywhere in one command
options.explanation: Glob can't find files by their content — it only matches file names and paths, not a key referenced inside them.

options.text: Grep to find the files that reference the key, then Edit to change each one
options.explanation: Correct — Grep locates the content match first, then a targeted edit tool changes just what's needed.

options.text: Read the entire codebase first, then Write each file back with the key renamed
options.explanation: This works but burns far more context reading every file than searching directly for the key.

options.text: Bash alone, piping `find` into a text-replacement command, since it's the only tool that can touch multiple files
options.explanation: The dedicated Grep and Edit tools already handle this more safely, without the shell-quoting concerns of scripting it through Bash.

keyPrinciple: Find matches by content with Grep first, then make targeted changes with Edit.

stem: You already know a bug is somewhere in `payment.ts`, but you're not sure which function causes it, so you want to follow the surrounding logic. Which tool fits best, and why not the alternative?

options.text: Grep — it returns every line, so it's equivalent to reading the whole file
options.explanation: Grep only returns lines matching a specific pattern, not the full surrounding context of the file.

options.text: Glob — it finds the file, and finding it counts as understanding it
options.explanation: Glob only matches the file's name or path — it doesn't show any content at all.

options.text: Read — it loads the full file and its surrounding logic; Grep would only return isolated lines
options.explanation: Correct — Read is the right tool when you need the whole picture, not just lines that match a pattern.

options.text: Write — since you'll need to fix the bug anyway, you might as well rewrite the whole file now
options.explanation: Write is for creating or replacing content, not for understanding a file before any change is decided.

keyPrinciple: Read loads a file's full content when you need to understand surrounding context, not just matching lines.

stem: You need to find every file whose name ends in `.stories.tsx`. Which tool matches this request?

options.text: Grep
options.explanation: Grep searches file contents, not filenames — nothing here is a text pattern to search for.

options.text: Read
options.explanation: Read loads one specific file's content — it can't find files by a name pattern.

options.text: Bash, since a shell command could technically do this
options.explanation: Bash could accomplish this, but the dedicated Glob tool is the direct, purpose-built match for a name pattern.

options.text: Glob
options.explanation: Correct — Glob matches file paths and names by pattern.

keyPrinciple: Glob finds files by name or path pattern.

stem: You want to check whether a newly written function actually compiles and its tests pass, not just visually inspect the code. Which built-in tool must be involved, and why can't Read alone answer this?

options.text: Bash — running the command is the only way to get real, executed output
options.explanation: Correct — only Bash executes a process; every other built-in tool just reads or writes file content.

options.text: Read — carefully re-reading the function is equivalent to compiling and running it
options.explanation: Reading the source can't reveal a runtime failure, a type error, or an environment issue — only actually running it can.

options.text: Grep — searching for `test(` calls confirms the tests pass
options.explanation: Finding test declarations says nothing about whether they actually pass when executed.

options.text: Edit — applying a small fix guarantees the function already compiles
options.explanation: Making an edit doesn't verify anything about the code's behavior — only running it does.

keyPrinciple: Bash is the only built-in tool that runs a process; the others only read or write files.

stem: A new file, `feature_flags.json`, doesn't exist yet and needs to be created with an initial set of ten flags. Which tool is correct, and why not the alternative?

options.text: Edit, because an empty, brand-new file is the easiest possible case for a unique-match anchor
options.explanation: Edit needs existing text to target — there's no content at all yet to anchor to.

options.text: Write — Edit needs existing text to target, and there's no content yet to anchor to
options.explanation: Correct — Write is for creating new files, exactly where Edit's unique-match requirement can't apply.

options.text: Glob, since it can create files matching a naming pattern
options.explanation: Glob only matches existing file names and paths — it never creates anything.

options.text: Bash, because only Bash can create files on disk
options.explanation: Bash could create a file via a shell redirect, but the dedicated Write tool is the direct, purpose-built choice for creating file content.

keyPrinciple: Use Write for new files or extensive rewrites; use Edit for small, targeted changes to existing content.

stem: An Edit call targets the snippet `if (user) { return true; }` inside a 400-line file. That exact block happens to appear in four different functions in the file. What will happen when this Edit call runs?

options.text: It will succeed regardless, always changing whichever occurrence it happens to find first from the top
options.explanation: Edit doesn't guess at a default occurrence — a non-unique match causes it to fail rather than pick one.

options.text: It will succeed, changing all four occurrences at once
options.explanation: Edit targets one unique match, not every occurrence of a repeated snippet.

options.text: It will fail without any change — the snippet isn't unique, and Edit won't guess which occurrence
options.explanation: Correct — Edit requires a unique match and fails cleanly rather than guessing when one doesn't exist.

options.text: It will succeed, but silently skip the file entirely
options.explanation: Edit reports a clear failure on a non-unique match rather than silently skipping anything.

keyPrinciple: Edit requires its target snippet to be unique in the file; a non-unique match fails rather than guessing.

stem: An Edit call to replace `const timeout = 5000;` fails because that exact line appears in three different config blocks in the same file. What's the reliable next step, instead of guessing at a longer anchor and retrying blindly?

options.text: Retry the same Edit call unchanged — it will succeed on a second attempt
options.explanation: An identical, still-ambiguous call fails the same way again; Edit doesn't behave differently on a retry.

options.text: Delete the file and recreate it from scratch with only the intended block
options.explanation: This discards content unnecessarily instead of preserving the file and changing only the intended part.

options.text: Switch to Bash and pipe the whole file through a text-replacement command instead of using Edit
options.explanation: This reintroduces the fragility — quoting, line-number drift — that the dedicated Read + Write fallback is meant to avoid.

options.text: Read the whole file, decide the right occurrence, then Write the updated content back
options.explanation: Correct — this is the documented, reliable fallback for a non-unique match.

keyPrinciple: When Edit fails on a non-unique match, use Read + Write as the reliable fallback.

stem: A script runs `Bash: grep -rn "TODO" .` across the repo to find leftover TODO comments, instead of using the dedicated Grep tool directly. On Windows machines on the team, this command behaves inconsistently. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Shelling out via Bash reintroduces cross-platform and quoting concerns Grep already handles safely
options.explanation: Correct — this is exactly the liability of reaching for Bash when a dedicated, purpose-built tool already exists.

options.text: `grep` cannot search multiple files at once, unlike the dedicated Grep tool
options.explanation: Shell `grep` can search multiple files; that's not the source of the Windows inconsistency.

options.text: Bash commands are only permitted on Linux and macOS machines, never on Windows
options.explanation: Bash commands do run on Windows in this environment — the issue is behavioral inconsistency, not a platform ban.

options.text: The dedicated Grep tool and the Bash `grep` command produce different match results for the same pattern
options.explanation: The problem described is cross-platform inconsistency of the shell command itself, not a difference in match results between the two tools.

keyPrinciple: Prefer the dedicated Grep/Glob tools over shelling out via Bash for plain content or path searches.

stem: A 300-line config file needs one boolean flag flipped from `false` to `true` on line 214. A teammate suggests reading the whole file and using Write to save it back with just that one flag changed. What's the downside compared to using Edit here?

options.text: Write cannot change boolean values, only strings
options.explanation: Write can save any content, including a changed boolean — that's not a real limitation.

options.text: Write reconstructs the entire file for a one-line change — a larger, less reviewable diff than Edit
options.explanation: Correct — Edit is the tighter, safer choice when the target text is unique, exactly this case.

options.text: Edit would first require deleting the existing file entirely, while Write does not need to do that
options.explanation: Edit never requires deleting a file — it modifies targeted text in place.

options.text: There's no real downside at all; Write and Edit are interchangeable for absolutely any change
options.explanation: They aren't interchangeable — Write's whole-file rewrite is a larger, less targeted change than Edit's surgical one.

keyPrinciple: Rewriting a whole file with Write for a small change is a larger, harder-to-review diff than a targeted Edit.

stem: `sendNotification` is defined in `notifications/core.ts`, then re-exported as `notify` from `notifications/index.ts`. Most of the codebase imports it as `notify`. A Grep search for callers of `sendNotification` alone turns up only two results, but the function is actually used in a dozen places. What went wrong, and what's the fix?

options.text: Nothing went wrong — two results means the function is barely used and can likely be removed
options.explanation: The two results only reflect callers that used the original name — they don't reflect the function's actual usage.

options.text: Grep can't search `.ts` files, so the missing results are a tooling limitation
options.explanation: Grep searches file contents regardless of extension — the missing results are about which name was searched for, not the file type.

options.text: The search only covered the original name; re-exported aliases need their own separate Grep pass
options.explanation: Correct — tracing usage through a wrapper module requires searching for every exported name, including aliases, not just the original.

options.text: The fix is to rename `sendNotification` to `notify` everywhere so only one name ever needs to be searched
options.explanation: This is a much larger change than the situation calls for, when simply searching for the existing alias already finds every caller.

keyPrinciple: To trace all callers through a wrapper or barrel module, first enumerate every exported name (including aliases), then Grep for each one.

stem: Your customer support agent's tools already have refined descriptions: `get_customer` — "Finds a customer by email (`user@domain.com`) or numeric `customer_id`. Returns profile and account status." `lookup_order` — "Finds an order by numeric `order_id`. Returns order status, items, and shipping info." Both descriptions state input formats and outputs. Production logs still show 9% of order-status questions like "is order 48213 on its way?" route to `get_customer` first. What is most likely still missing from these descriptions, and what's the fix?

options.text: Neither description states when to prefer it over the other tool; add a one-sentence boundary noting `get_customer` is for identity/account lookups and `lookup_order` is for anything keyed by an order number.
options.explanation: Correct. Both tools already have input formats and outputs, so the remaining gap is the boundary statement — exactly the ingredient that tells the model which tool to prefer given overlapping request phrasing.

options.text: Neither description lists example queries; add 3-4 example user phrasings to each tool description so the model pattern-matches on wording.
options.explanation: Examples reinforce specific phrasings but don't state the actual decision rule (an order number present means `lookup_order`, regardless of other wording) — the more direct fix is a boundary statement, not more phrasing samples.

options.text: The descriptions don't yet specify edge cases, such as what happens when an `order_id` doesn't exist; add edge-case handling notes to both tools.
options.explanation: Edge-case handling is a real ingredient of a good description, but it addresses a different problem (what happens after a tool is called), not which tool gets selected in the first place.

options.text: The input formats aren't precise enough; tighten the `customer_id` and `order_id` format constraints in each schema so the model can validate them before calling, even though neither ID was actually malformed in the failing requests.
options.explanation: The formats are already distinct and stated; tightening schema validation doesn't change which tool the model reaches for when a request doesn't explicitly name an ID.

keyPrinciple: Even with input formats stated, overlapping tools still need an explicit boundary sentence saying when to prefer one over the other.
sourceRef: Exam Guide TS 2.1; guide_en.md §2.2; Exam Guide Sample Q2

stem: Your research system's document-analysis agent has one tool, `analyze_document`: "Analyzes an uploaded document and returns insights including key data points, a summary, and claim verification against the source text." Logs show that when researchers ask "just summarize this doc," "pull out the stats," or "check if this claim is true," the agent's single call still returns all three kinds of output every time, wasting tokens and confusing downstream synthesis. What's the most effective redesign?

options.text: Add a parameter to `analyze_document`'s input schema letting the caller specify which output type it wants (data points, summary, or verification), keeping one tool but requiring the model to fill that parameter correctly on every single call.
options.explanation: A real pattern in some cases, but it still leaves one generic tool whose purpose the model must reason about correctly filling a parameter for, rather than three self-evidently distinct tools with narrow contracts.

options.text: Split `analyze_document` into three tools — `extract_data_points`, `summarize_content`, and `verify_claim_against_source` — each with a narrow, defined output contract.
options.explanation: Correct. This is the documented fix for a generic tool covering unrelated jobs: give each responsibility its own tool with a defined input/output contract, so the model's choice of tool name already determines the output shape.

options.text: Rewrite the single description as a bulleted list stating exactly which response section applies to summary vs. data vs. verification requests.
options.explanation: The tool still returns one blob per call regardless of what the caller asked for — rewriting the description doesn't change that the backend keeps producing all three outputs together.

options.text: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt showing three sample requests, each paired with the specific output type expected.
options.explanation: This targets tool-selection wording, but the actual problem is that the tool itself returns everything regardless of intent — few-shot examples don't change what the single tool call produces.

keyPrinciple: Split a generic, multi-purpose tool into purpose-specific tools with defined input/output contracts.

stem: A developer-productivity agent has two clearly, distinctly described tools: `run_tests` and `run_linter` (the latter's description explicitly covers formatting checks). Its system prompt includes: "Whenever the user mentions 'check' or 'verify' the code, run the test suite first." Logs show requests like "can you verify the formatting is correct" trigger `run_tests` instead of `run_linter` 22% of the time. What's the most effective fix?

options.text: Rename `run_linter` to `check_formatting` so it visually matches the trigger keyword "check."
options.explanation: Renaming can remove overlap between two similarly-purposed tools, but it doesn't stop the system prompt's blanket rule, which fires on the word "verify" regardless of what the linter tool is named.

options.text: Remove the system-prompt instruction entirely and rely fully on `tool_choice: "auto"` with no guidance, trusting the already-good tool descriptions alone to carry every routing decision.
options.explanation: This would likely fix this specific symptom, but it overcorrects by removing useful guidance for the legitimate cases where running tests first genuinely is the right call — too blunt an instrument.

options.text: Rewrite the system-prompt instruction so it isn't a blanket keyword trigger on "check/verify," but instead routes based on what's being checked (tests vs. formatting/lint rules).
options.explanation: Correct. The tools are already well described; the actual cause is a keyword-sensitive instruction overriding that description. Fixing the instruction to key off the actual subject of the request (not a loose keyword) addresses the root cause without discarding guidance entirely.

options.text: Expand `run_linter`'s description with more edge cases and examples.
options.explanation: The descriptions already clearly differentiate the two tools; the misrouting is caused by the system prompt overriding that distinction, not by ambiguity in the descriptions themselves.

keyPrinciple: Keyword-sensitive system prompt wording can override even well-written, well-differentiated tool descriptions — review the prompt, not just the tools.

stem: Your `process_refund` MCP tool succeeds for refunds under the $500 policy limit. For refunds over the limit, the backend correctly rejects the request as requiring manager approval, but the tool currently returns `{"isError": true, "content": "Operation failed"}` in both success-path failures and this policy rejection. The support agent responds inconsistently: sometimes retrying the identical refund three times, sometimes telling the customer "system error, try again later." How should this specific case (a refund correctly rejected for exceeding the policy threshold) be represented, including the retry flag?

options.text: `isError:true`, `errorCategory:"validation"`, `isRetryable:false`, with a generic message, since the refund amount technically fails a checked constraint the same way a malformed field would.
options.explanation: Validation errors are for malformed or invalid input that can be fixed and resubmitted; this refund request was well-formed and was correctly rejected by a policy rule, which is the business category, not validation.

options.text: `isError:true`, `errorCategory:"business"`, `isRetryable:false`, with a message explaining the $500 threshold, so the agent can explain the policy instead of retrying or reporting a generic system error.
options.explanation: Correct. The request was valid and was correctly rejected by a business rule (the policy threshold); categorizing it as business with isRetryable:false and a clear explanation lets the agent communicate the reason instead of retrying or misreporting it as a system failure.

options.text: `isError:true`, `errorCategory:"transient"`, `isRetryable:true`, so the agent can retry after the manager approval workflow completes.
options.explanation: Retrying the identical refund call will not make a manager approval appear — this isn't a timeout or service outage, so marking it retryable actively misleads the agent into wasting further calls.

options.text: `isError:false`, with an empty content body and a separate `requires_approval` status field outside the standard error shape, so downstream logging can key off that field instead.
options.explanation: This avoids using the isError/errorCategory mechanism the agent already relies on to recognize failures, inventing a nonstandard shape instead of the documented structured-error pattern.

keyPrinciple: A correctly-rejected policy violation on a valid request is a business error (isRetryable:false with a clear explanation), not validation or transient.

stem: A `fetch_source_document` MCP tool, used by the document-analysis agent, hits a permission-denied error when trying to access a paywalled internal document. It currently returns `isError:true`, `errorCategory:"transient"`, `isRetryable:true`. The agent retries 5 times with exponential backoff, always failing identically, adding several seconds of latency before giving up. What's the most effective fix?

options.text: The error is miscategorized; it should be `errorCategory:"permission"`, `isRetryable:false`, so the agent escalates instead of retrying an access failure that retrying cannot fix.
options.explanation: Correct. Permission-denied failures don't resolve by retrying with the same credentials — recategorizing to permission with isRetryable:false lets the agent escalate immediately instead of burning retries on a failure mode retries can never fix.

options.text: The retry count is too high; keep `errorCategory:"transient"` but cap local retries at 1-2 instead of 5 before propagating.
options.explanation: Bounded local retries are the right pattern for genuinely transient failures, but capping the count here still wastes calls on a permission failure that can never succeed on retry, and leaves the category internally inconsistent for future permission errors from this tool.

options.text: The tool should catch the permission error and return an empty result set marked as successful, so the research pipeline continues without stalling or waiting on this one inaccessible source.
options.explanation: This silently converts a real access failure into what looks like "no matches," hiding a source that was never actually checked from the coverage picture the coordinator relies on.

options.text: The error category is fine as `"transient"`, but `isRetryable` should be set to `false` so the agent doesn't waste further calls.
options.explanation: Half right — isRetryable:false does stop the wasted retries, but leaving the category as "transient" is internally inconsistent and misleads anyone (or anything) that reads the category field to decide how to respond to future failures from this tool.

keyPrinciple: Match the error category to the actual failure mode — a permission failure needs escalation, and retry tuning alone doesn't fix a wrong category.

stem: `lookup_order` returns no matching order when a customer's stated order number genuinely has no record. Separately, the backend order-lookup service is sometimes unreachable entirely. Both currently produce an identical response: `isError:false`, `content: {"orders": []}`. During a recent outage, support agents told customers "we found no record of that order" even though the service simply couldn't be reached. What's the fix?

options.text: Always return `isError:true` whenever the result array is empty, regardless of cause, so the agent treats every no-match case as something to retry or escalate before answering the customer.
options.explanation: This overcorrects: it makes the common, correct case (a genuine, successful zero-match query) look like a failure too, which would cause the agent to retry or escalate perfectly normal "no such order" responses.

options.text: Keep the empty array for genuine zero-match queries only; return `isError:true`, `errorCategory:"transient"`, `isRetryable:true` instead when the backend is unreachable.
options.explanation: Correct. This preserves the empty array as a valid, successful result when there truly are no matches, while giving the unreachable-backend case its own distinct, structured error shape the agent can act on — retry or inform the customer of a system issue, not a missing order.

options.text: Add a warning field alongside the empty array, e.g. `"results_may_be_incomplete": true`, whenever there's ambiguity, while keeping `isError:false` in both cases.
options.explanation: A soft warning field is better than nothing, but keeping `isError:false` for a real access failure still doesn't give the agent the categorical isError/isRetryable signal it needs to decide to retry rather than just note a caveat.

options.text: Have `lookup_order` retry internally up to 5 times on backend unavailability before returning any response, so the caller only ever sees a final, confirmed empty array.
options.explanation: This just delays the same ambiguity — after retries exhaust, the caller still can't tell whether a final empty array means "no results" or "still couldn't reach the service," and it does so only after added latency.

keyPrinciple: A valid empty result and an access failure must never share the same response shape — only one of them is actually isError:true.

stem: A research coordinator has 4 subagents. The synthesis agent has been given all 14 tools from the web-search and document-analysis agents "for flexibility," in addition to its own 3 synthesis tools — 17 tools total. Logs show the synthesis agent occasionally calls a web-search tool directly instead of asking the coordinator to delegate, and sometimes passes malformed input meant for a document-analysis tool into the wrong schema. What's the most effective fix?

options.text: Keep all 17 tools, but add a system-prompt instruction telling the synthesis agent "only use tools 15-17 (your own); do not call the others."
options.explanation: This attempts to scope behavior through a prompt instead of through the tool list itself — the borrowed tools are still present and selectable, so the model can still violate a soft instruction under the right phrasing.

options.text: Reduce the borrowed tools from 14 to 7 by removing the least-used half, keeping the more frequently useful web-search and document tools available.
options.explanation: This trims the count but still leaves roughly 10 tools on an agent whose actual role needs only 3, and every remaining borrowed tool is still an opportunity for role drift — it addresses the number, not the underlying role-boundary violation.

options.text: Remove the borrowed tools, leaving only the synthesis agent's 3 role-specific tools, and route cross-role needs through the coordinator.
options.explanation: Correct. This restricts the synthesis agent's tool set to exactly what its role needs, removing the opportunity for cross-specialization misuse rather than trying to suppress it with instructions or partial trimming.

options.text: Keep all 17 tools, but set `tool_choice` to force one of the 3 synthesis tools on the synthesis agent's first turn only, leaving every later turn on `tool_choice: "auto"` across the full 17-tool list.
options.explanation: Forcing a synthesis tool on the first turn does nothing about the 14 borrowed tools still being freely selectable on every subsequent turn.

keyPrinciple: Scope an agent's tool list to its role directly — a prompt instruction or partial trim still leaves misuse opportunities that removing the tools entirely does not.

stem: At the end of a resolved support conversation, your agent must always produce a structured logging call — never a plain-text closing message — using whichever of two tools matches the actual outcome: `case_summary` (for resolved cases) or `escalation_summary` (for cases handed to a human). Which `tool_choice` setting is correct for this final turn?

options.text: `{"type": "tool", "name": "case_summary"}`, forcing `case_summary` specifically, so every conversation produces a consistent single logging format.
options.explanation: Forced selection guarantees structure, but it forces the wrong tool whenever the case was actually escalated — forced selection is for guaranteeing one specific tool, not for choosing between two valid outcomes.

options.text: `{"type": "auto"}`, since the model reliably calls a summary tool once a case is resolved, and forcing anything risks blocking legitimate plain-text follow-up questions the customer might still have.
options.explanation: "auto" still permits the model to end with plain text instead of a tool call — exactly the failure this design needs to avoid, since a structured log entry is required every time.

options.text: `{"type": "any"}` combined with removing `escalation_summary` from the tool list, so there is only one possible structured output.
options.explanation: This reaches a guaranteed structured call, but by removing `escalation_summary` it also destroys the ability to ever log an escalation correctly — over-fitting the guarantee to only one of the two real outcomes.

options.text: `{"type": "any"}`, so the model must call one of the two summary tools rather than end with a plain-text reply, while still choosing whichever matches the actual outcome.
options.explanation: Correct. "any" guarantees a tool call happens (ruling out a plain-text close) while still letting the model pick between `case_summary` and `escalation_summary` based on what actually happened — exactly the guarantee needed here.

keyPrinciple: Use tool_choice: "any" when you need a guaranteed tool call but the correct tool depends on which of several valid outcomes applies.

stem: A developer-productivity agent has a generic `run_command` tool that executes arbitrary shell strings the model composes, used for everything from running tests to fetching internal wiki pages via `curl`. Logs show it occasionally composes a slightly wrong `curl` invocation against an internal doc server (missing auth headers, wrong path pattern), separate from its legitimate, reliable use for build and test commands. What's the most effective redesign?

options.text: Keep `run_command` for build/test/git needs, but replace the doc-fetching use case with a constrained `load_internal_doc` tool that validates the path and attaches auth automatically.
options.explanation: Correct. This targets the specific failure mode — hand-composed, error-prone `curl` calls — with a constrained, validated tool, while leaving the agent's genuinely needed general command capability intact for the tasks it's already handling reliably.

options.text: Add a system-prompt rule instructing the model to always double-check `curl` syntax and never run destructive commands during cleanup requests, without changing what the tool is structurally still allowed to execute.
options.explanation: This is a probabilistic instruction layered on top of a structurally unconstrained tool — it may reduce errors somewhat but doesn't remove the underlying ability to keep hand-composing incorrect calls.

options.text: Replace `run_command` entirely with two narrower tools, `run_tests` and `run_build`, removing shell access altogether.
options.explanation: This overcorrects: it removes shell capability the agent genuinely needs for other legitimate build/test/git work described in the scenario, when the actual problem is isolated to the doc-fetching use case.

options.text: Keep `run_command` as-is, but add a confirmation step that shows the composed command to a human before every execution.
options.explanation: This adds a human-in-the-loop bottleneck to every call, including the routine, already-reliable build and test invocations, rather than fixing the tool boundary for the one risky use case.

keyPrinciple: Replace a generic tool with a constrained alternative for the specific misuse pattern, rather than removing capability broadly or relying on prompt-level caution.

stem: Your team's `.mcp.json`, committed to the repo, has `"env": { "GITHUB_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}" }`. A new teammate who hasn't set `GITHUB_TOKEN` in their own shell reports the GitHub MCP server "half-works": `claude mcp list` shows a missing-variable warning, and GitHub tools fail when called. A colleague suggests hardcoding a shared bot token directly into `.mcp.json` so onboarding is instant. What's the best response?

options.text: Hardcode a shared bot token into `.mcp.json` now, and rotate it later once onboarding stabilizes.
options.explanation: This commits a literal credential into version control — exactly what environment variable expansion exists to prevent — and "rotate later" doesn't undo the exposure already in git history.

options.text: Don't hardcode the token; have the teammate set `GITHUB_TOKEN` in their own environment, keeping `.mcp.json` unchanged and secret-free.
options.explanation: Correct. `.mcp.json` is designed to stay secret-free and shared; each developer supplies their own token through their own environment, which is exactly what the missing-variable warning is telling the new teammate to do.

options.text: Move the GitHub server config out of `.mcp.json` into each teammate's `~/.claude.json` so everyone sets their own token locally.
options.explanation: This solves the credential problem by turning a shared, version-controlled server definition into a private, per-developer one — now new teammates must recreate the whole server entry themselves, not just supply a token.

options.text: Add the shared token as a fallback default directly in the expansion syntax (e.g. `${GITHUB_TOKEN:-<shared token value>}`), so the server works even before a teammate configures their own token.
options.explanation: Using a real shared credential as a fallback default re-embeds that credential into the committed file — a fallback default should be a safe, non-secret value, not a working token.

keyPrinciple: Environment variable expansion in .mcp.json exists so credentials live in each developer's own environment, never in the committed file itself.

stem: A developer-productivity agent connects to an internal wiki MCP server exposing tools like `search_wiki` and `get_page`. To answer "what internal documentation exists about the deployment pipeline," the agent currently issues 6-8 exploratory `search_wiki` calls with different keyword guesses before finding the right page. The wiki server also exposes a `docs://index` resource listing every page title and its section hierarchy. What's the most effective way to reduce this exploratory overhead?

options.text: Improve `search_wiki`'s description with more example queries so the model's first guess is more likely to hit the right keyword, cutting down wasted follow-up searches.
options.explanation: This can improve the odds of a lucky first search, but it doesn't remove the fundamental guess-and-check pattern — the agent still has to search rather than simply look up the answer from an available catalog.

options.text: Increase the number of results `search_wiki` returns per call, so fewer repeated searches are needed to find the right page.
options.explanation: This reduces the retry count somewhat but doesn't remove the underlying guesswork about what keywords to search for in the first place.

options.text: Have the agent read the `docs://index` resource first, then make one targeted `get_page` call instead of repeated keyword-guessing searches.
options.explanation: Correct. Resources exist precisely to expose a content catalog the agent can read directly, without spending exploratory tool calls — one resource read replaces the multi-call guessing pattern.

options.text: Add a `list_all_pages` tool alongside `search_wiki`, so the model can call it first to see titles before searching.
options.explanation: This is functionally close to reading the resource, but it's a redundant tool call the model must still choose to make and pay a round trip for, duplicating a catalog the server already exposes more cheaply as a resource.

keyPrinciple: Expose content catalogs as MCP resources so agents can see what data exists without exploratory tool calls.

stem: Your team already uses a community-maintained MCP server for Jira (search, create, comment). A developer proposes writing a custom in-house MCP server to replace it, arguing it would let them add one company-specific feature — auto-linking Jira tickets to internal deploy IDs — alongside the standard operations. What's the most effective approach?

options.text: Replace the community server entirely with a custom one that reimplements all standard Jira operations plus the new linking feature, for a single unified integration.
options.explanation: This takes on ongoing maintenance of standard Jira operations (auth, pagination, API version changes) that the community server already tracks for free — exactly the effort a custom server should be reserved from.

options.text: Fork the community server's source and add the linking feature directly inside it, maintaining the fork going forward.
options.explanation: This creates a recurring maintenance cost — merging upstream changes into the fork indefinitely — for the sake of one small, team-specific feature.

options.text: Keep using the community server unmodified, and have developers manually cross-reference deploy IDs until a future review decides whether custom tooling is warranted.
options.explanation: This avoids any engineering cost but leaves a known, recurring manual step unaddressed indefinitely, rather than solving it with a proportionate fix.

options.text: Keep the community Jira server for standard operations, and build a small, separate custom MCP server that exposes just the deploy-ID linking feature.
options.explanation: Correct. This keeps the community server doing what it already does well, and reserves custom development for the one genuinely team-specific capability — the proportionate application of "prefer community servers for standard integrations, build custom only for team-specific workflows."

keyPrinciple: Reserve custom MCP servers for genuinely team-specific features; keep community servers for standard integrations rather than reimplementing or forking them.

stem: A developer-productivity agent is asked: "Find every file that imports the deprecated `LegacyLogger` module so I can migrate them." Which approach correctly answers this request?

options.text: Use Grep to search file contents for `LegacyLogger` import statements, since the target is text inside files, not a filename pattern.
options.explanation: Correct. The request is about where a specific string (an import of `LegacyLogger`) appears inside files, which is exactly what Grep is for.

options.text: Use Glob with `**/*LegacyLogger*` to find every file whose name contains "LegacyLogger," then read each result, assuming importing files are named similarly to what they import.
options.explanation: This only finds files literally named after LegacyLogger — it misses every file that imports the module under an unrelated filename, which is almost certainly most of the actual callers.

options.text: Use Glob to find all `.ts` files, then Read each one in full to check for a `LegacyLogger` import.
options.explanation: This would eventually work, but it reads every TypeScript file's full content instead of searching directly for the text — a much more token-expensive path to the same answer Grep gives directly.

options.text: Use Bash with `grep -r "LegacyLogger" .` from the project root, piping the output to a file for review.
options.explanation: This produces functionally similar results to using the dedicated Grep tool, but it reintroduces shell-quoting and cross-platform concerns for a job the built-in Grep tool already handles more directly.

keyPrinciple: Grep searches file contents for a pattern; Glob only matches file names and paths.

stem: A developer-productivity agent needs to find out who last modified a specific function and why, to understand context before refactoring it. Which approach correctly answers this?

options.text: Grep the file for a comment block near the function that might explain its history.
options.explanation: A comment, if one even exists, reflects only what someone chose to write down at some point — it isn't authorship or commit-message history, and Grep has no access to version-control metadata at all.

options.text: Use Bash to run `git blame -L <lines> <file>`, which reports commit authorship and message per line.
options.explanation: Correct. Authorship and commit history are version-control metadata that only exist by running git itself — Bash is the only built-in tool that executes a process, and git blame is exactly the process that answers this question.

options.text: Read the file's full history by opening every past commit's version of the file and diffing them manually.
options.explanation: This could theoretically reconstruct the history, but it's a slow, manual reimplementation of what a single `git blame` command already reports directly — and Read alone can't retrieve past commit versions without Bash running git commands anyway.

options.text: Glob for files with similar names to find a changelog or docs file that might describe the change.
options.explanation: This depends on a changelog happening to exist and to be current and specific enough to answer the question — an unreliable proxy for the actual, authoritative commit history that a real git command retrieves directly.

keyPrinciple: Bash is required for anything that depends on running a real process — including git commands like blame or log — since no other built-in tool executes anything.

stem: While refactoring, the agent tries to use Edit to replace `const timeout = 3000;` with `const timeout = 5000;` inside `config.ts`, but the call fails: the exact string `const timeout = 3000;` appears in three different exported config objects in the same file, and Edit reports it cannot determine which occurrence to change. What is the correct next step?

options.text: Retry Edit with the exact same snippet a second time; Edit will pick the first occurrence by default if the same call is repeated.
options.explanation: Edit has no such default-to-first-occurrence retry behavior — an identical ambiguous call reports the same non-unique-match failure again.

options.text: Use Grep to find the line numbers of all three occurrences, then use Bash with a text-processing command to replace only the line at the specific line number.
options.explanation: This can work, but it swaps the safe, integrated Read + Write fallback for shell text manipulation, reintroducing exactly the fragility (line-number drift, quoting) that the dedicated fallback exists to avoid.

options.text: Read the full file, determine which of the three occurrences is the correct one from surrounding context, then Write the file back with only that occurrence changed.
options.explanation: Correct. This is the documented fallback for a non-unique match: Read the whole file to see all the context, decide the right occurrence with certainty, then Write the corrected content back.

options.text: Retry Edit with a longer snippet that includes a few extra surrounding lines, without first reading the file to check whether that longer snippet is actually unique across all three occurrences.
options.explanation: This is guessing at uniqueness blind — the longer snippet might still match more than one occurrence, or might accidentally be unique but around the wrong one, since the file was never actually inspected first.

keyPrinciple: When Edit fails on a non-unique match, read the file first to confirm which occurrence is correct, rather than guessing at a longer anchor blind.

stem: You're asked to add a new field to an API response in a codebase you don't know. What is the most efficient way to start investigating where the change belongs?

options.text: Read every file under `src/api/` in full first, to build complete context before deciding where the change belongs.
options.explanation: This is thorough, but it's the token- and time-expensive anti-pattern of reading everything upfront, when a targeted search would locate the relevant file(s) directly.

options.text: Glob for `**/*.ts` under the project root to get a full file listing, then Read each file whose name sounds related to "api" or "response," hoping the naming lines up with the actual logic.
options.explanation: This narrows by guessing from filenames alone and still reads multiple files speculatively — a plausible-sounding name doesn't confirm the file actually builds the response in question.

options.text: Use Bash to run a project-wide `wc -l` on all source files first, to identify the largest files as the most likely place for core logic.
options.explanation: File size has no reliable connection to where a specific response-building function lives, and this approach doesn't use any tool built for finding relevant code by name or content.

options.text: Grep for the existing response-building function's name or the API route path to find the relevant file(s) first, then Read just those files before making any change.
options.explanation: Correct. This is the incremental investigation pattern: search by content for a concrete entry point first, then read only the files that search confirms are relevant, instead of reading or guessing broadly.

keyPrinciple: Build codebase understanding incrementally — Grep for entry points, then Read just the files that search confirms are relevant.

stem: After editing a function, the agent needs to confirm the existing unit tests still pass before reporting the task as done. Which tool call actually answers that question?

options.text: Bash: run the project's test command (e.g. `npm test`) and check the exit code and output.
options.explanation: Correct. Whether tests pass depends on actually executing them — Bash is the only built-in tool that runs a process and can report the real result.

options.text: Read the test file for the edited function and manually verify the assertions look consistent with the new implementation.
options.explanation: This is reasoning about likely correctness from static content, but it can't catch a real runtime failure — a typo, a type error, or an environment issue — that only actually running the tests would reveal.

options.text: Grep the edited file for `TODO` or `FIXME` markers to confirm no known issues were left behind.
options.explanation: The presence or absence of markers says nothing about whether the test suite passes — this checks for an unrelated signal.

options.text: Glob for `*.test.ts` files related to the edited module to confirm test coverage exists for this function.
options.explanation: Confirming that tests exist is not the same as confirming they pass — this answers a different question than the one asked.

keyPrinciple: Only Bash executes a real process; use it whenever the answer depends on actually running something, like a test suite.

stem: `formatCurrency` is defined in `src/utils/currency.ts`, then re-exported as `money` from `src/utils/index.ts` (`export { formatCurrency as money } from './currency'`). Elsewhere in the codebase, components import `{ money }` from the barrel file and never reference `formatCurrency` directly. You need to find every call site before changing its signature. Grepping for `formatCurrency` across the codebase returns only the definition and the re-export line. What should you do next?

options.text: Conclude that `formatCurrency` has no other call sites and is safe to change, since the Grep search already covered the whole codebase and returned only the definition and the re-export line.
options.explanation: This is the failure mode the scenario is illustrating: the search covered the whole codebase for one specific string, but every real caller imports the re-exported alias `money`, which never contains the text "formatCurrency" at all.

options.text: Grep separately for `money` (the re-exported alias) across the codebase, since call sites that only import the barrel file's export will never contain the string "formatCurrency."
options.explanation: Correct. Tracing usage through a wrapper or barrel module requires first identifying every exported name (including aliases), then searching for each one — searching only the original definition name misses alias-only call sites.

options.text: Re-run the same Grep for `formatCurrency` restricted to `**/*.tsx` files only, in case the first search missed frontend components.
options.explanation: Narrowing the file scope doesn't help — the search is still for the string "formatCurrency," which alias-only call sites never contain, regardless of which file types are included.

options.text: Use Glob to find every file named `*currency*` or `*money*`, then Read each one fully to check for usages.
options.explanation: This might stumble onto the barrel file itself by luck, but it's an unreliable, filename-guessing approach to a content-tracing problem, and it will miss call sites in files that don't happen to have "currency" or "money" in their own names.

keyPrinciple: To trace all callers of a function through a wrapper or barrel module, first enumerate every exported name (including aliases), then Grep for each one separately.
